title: memory-fragmentation-oom-root-cause-triage-2026-03-04
content:
Summary:

These notes capture the triage of intermittent OOMs and memory fragmentation observed in the serving runtime (hosted + dedicated). The failures typically occur under moderate-to-high concurrent request churn for medium-length sequences (512-2048) and after long uptime (~hours). Goal: document observed allocator behavior, root causes, reproduction steps, mitigations, and action items.

High-level findings:
- The dominant vector is allocator-level fragmentation caused by frequent variable-sized workspace allocations and repeated cudaMalloc/cudaFree patterns from third-party libs and kernels.
- The runtime’s current per-request allocation pattern (allocate workspace -> run kernels -> free) combined with concurrent requests leads to many small lifetimes that break up large free ranges.
- CUDA driver/cudaMalloc has internal bookkeeping and alignment constraints that make freed regions not always mergeable in practice, leading to free-list fragmentation and inability to satisfy a subsequent large allocation even though total free memory > requested size.
- KV cache growth and pinning (per-session long-lived allocations) reduce available large contiguous regions. The combination of many pinned small allocations and transient mid-size allocations is the worst-case.

Tools & signals used:
- nsys (Nsight Systems) traces for timeline visualization of alloc/free patterns and kernel launches.
- NVTX annotations around allocator calls (we added temporary annotations).
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free,utilization.gpu --loop-ms to sample HWM and free memory.
- NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) through dcgm for finer sampling in production tests.
- cuda-memcheck for correctness when exercising pooling changes.
- Custom allocator telemetry (counts, sizes, histograms) exported via runtime metrics endpoint.
- Repro harness: synthetic workload generator that stimulates 50–150 concurrent sessions, mix of short (32–128 tokens) and medium (512–2048) sequences to reproduce fragmentation within 30–90 minutes.

Reproduction notes (short):
1) Start a dedicated serving node with current runtime build (no pooling except PyTorch caching allocator).
2) Run synthetic clients at 100 qps with concurrency 60, sequence length distribution: 70% short, 30% medium.
3) Observe memory usage rising and HWM creeping; after ~40–90 minutes either: a) a large workspace allocation fails (cudaMalloc returns OOM) despite free memory reported by nvidia-smi, or b) process hits an OOM and is restarted by supervisor.
4) Capture an nsys trace at the time of failure.

Allocator behavior observed:
- Two allocation classes present: long-lived pinned buffers (KV cache arrays, persistent buffers) and many short-lived workspaces used by kernels (attention, dropout, cuBLAS heuristics).
- Short-lived allocations are often mid-sized (hundreds of KB to tens of MB) and vary across kernels and sequence length.
- When many concurrent requests interleave allocations and frees, the free ranges break into small fragments. Later a large contiguous workspace allocation (e.g., for dense matmul or fused kernel with batch*seq*hidden_bytes) fails because no single free block is big enough even though sum(free) > needed.
- The CUDA driver does some internal coalescing but not aggressively enough for our patterns. Frequent cudaFree followed by immediate cudaMalloc exacerbates the issue.

Example trace highlights (from nsys 2026-02-18 run):
- t=00:12:03: several kernels free ~20MB blocks each from prior inference requests.
- t=00:12:05: multiple requests request a 60MB workspace; CUDA returns OOM for the first, then smaller allocations succeed.
- Histogram of allocation sizes: spike at ~512KB (many small aux buffers), broad mass 1–32MB (workspaces), rare large >128MB (rare model initialization).
- Fragmentation metric (live free ranges) shows average free-range size dropping from ~64MB to ~8MB before failure.

Root causes (prioritized):
1) Transient per-request workspace allocation pattern (no pre-reserved workspace pool) causing frequent cudaMalloc/cudaFree churn and fragmentation.
2) Long-lived allocations (KV caches, gradient buffers in some also-instrumented paths) scatter pinned pages and reduce contiguous free regions.
3) Mixed allocation sizes and concurrency create classic external fragmentation; CUDA driver doesn't compact/free-on-demand to satisfy large contiguous request.
4) Some third-party kernels/libraries internally call cudaMalloc for temporary workspace (e.g., custom fused ops or cuDNN heuristics) which we cannot control without interception/pooling.

Mitigations tried (results):
- Preallocated global per-GPU heap (single large cudaMalloc) + suballocator: good improvement. When we switched to a large prealloc (e.g., reserve 90% of GPU) and implemented a simple slab/buddy suballocator we eliminated the observed OOMs in the repro harness for >6 hours.
  - Pros: contiguous address space is guaranteed within our managed region; very low fragmentation with size-segregated pools.
  - Cons: reduced visibility to driver-level allocation failures; needs careful safety when other processes share GPU (not our deployment for Dedicated nodes).
- Use PyTorch caching allocator for everything: partially helpful for PyTorch-based kernels but not for native cudaMalloc calls from third-party libs.
- Pinning policy: reduce lifetime of long-lived but sparse allocations by consolidating per-session small buffers into a single packed buffer per-session. This improved contiguous free-region sizes by 20–40%.
- Align/round-up allocation sizes to power-of-two classes (slab-like): reduced fragmentation further.
- Limit concurrency and add backpressure: reduces churn and delays fragmentation onset, but affects latency/SLOs.
- cuMallocAsync / cuMemPool API: tested on CUDA 11.2+ in lab. cuMallocAsync with cuMemPool and stream-local pools shows promising reduction in fragmentation and latency for transient allocations. However: not uniformly available on all node OS images we use; requires driver >= certain versions; requires careful pool sizing to avoid cross-stream contention.

Recommended immediate mitigations (short-term):
1) Implement a preallocated GPU heap + runtime suballocator (size-segregated) behind a feature flag. Roll out to Dedicated nodes first. Rationale: deterministic improvement and fast mitigation for production OOMs.
2) Intercept known third-party cudaMalloc calls where possible (wrap allocator at runtime) and route them through our suballocator. Add NVTX annotations for visibility.
3) Consolidate per-session small persistent buffers into a packed region to reduce number of long-lived allocations.
4) Tune default workspace sizes to be conservative (slightly smaller) and enable request-level fallback to smaller math kernels when large workspace allocation fails.

Recommended medium-term changes (3-6 months):
1) Evaluate cuMallocAsync/cuMemPool adoption across our fleet. Build automated validation/test images with required drivers and run stress tests. cuMallocAsync looks like the right long-term upstream approach.
2) Improve allocator telemetry (per-range histograms, fragmentation ratio, largest-free-block) exposed to Console. This lets customers and SREs detect fragmentation onset earlier and take actions (node restart or workload migration).
3) Kernel owners: audit kernels that call cudaMalloc internally (esp. fused/custom ops and some vendor libs) and prefer pooled APIs.
4) Per-model workspace calculators: compute conservative upper bounds (peak workspace per-batch/seq) and allow a runtime-mode that pre-reserves per-model workspace at load time.

Open questions / risks:
- Preallocation reduces memory available to other tenants/processes on shared machines. For Dedicated nodes this is acceptable; for multi-tenant hosted nodes we need a less intrusive approach.
- cuMallocAsync adoption requires driver/OS standardization; rolling this fleet-wide requires coordination with infra and release-engineering.
- Suballocator correctness: need thorough testing (race conditions, memory leaks) under high concurrency.

Planned experiments (next 2 weeks):
- A/B test: current allocator vs. prealloc+suballocator on two identical Dedicated nodes under the same synthetic load for 24h. Metrics: time-to-fragmentation, HWM, number of OOM failures, latency p99.
- Smoke test of cuMallocAsync on a small pool of nodes with driver 535+: compare fragmentation metrics and latency for transient allocations.
- Launch a telemetry dashboard for fragmentation metrics (largest free block over time) for a subset of production serving hosts.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: implement feature-flagged prealloc+suballocator prototype, add NVTX around allocator paths (due: 2026-03-11).
- Miguel: consolidate per-session small buffers into packed allocation API and prepare migration plan for model init (due: 2026-03-18).
- Priya: run cuMallocAsync compatibility matrix against current fleet images and document required driver/kernel versions (due: 2026-03-10).
- Evan: add fragmentation telemetry and dashboard prototype (due: 2026-03-17).

Appendix: quick mitigations checklist for on-call
- If node hits repeated OOMs: drain node, rotate traffic, reboot (as last resort).
- If fragmentation alerts triggered: reduce concurrency for that worker pool (scale-in), enable conservative workspace mode for models, or move high-concurrency customers to Dedicated capacity.
- Capture nsys trace and allocator metrics snapshot before restart.

Notes: These are working notes; will convert critical parts to a Confluence post and a runbook once we validate the prealloc approach in the A/B test.

-- end --
